prompt: Which command produces the displayed default route?
options: ip default-gateway 10.0.12.2
explanation: The destination and mask are both zero, identifying /0. The next hop is 10.0.12.2.

whyWrong.0: ip default-gateway serves host-mode management; it does not create this static route on an IP-routing router.
whyWrong.1: A /32 identifies one address, not a default.
whyWrong.2: This names the transit subnet as the destination and does not create a default.

prompt: A floating static is configured but loses to a healthy primary route. Which command directly shows the configured backup line?
options: show ip route static
show interfaces
show running-config
show ip arp
explanation: The running configuration includes configured candidates even when they are not selected into the routing table.

whyWrong.0: This filters installed routes and normally omits the losing floating candidate.
whyWrong.1: Interface details do not list static-route statements.
whyWrong.3: ARP shows address-resolution entries, not configured routes.

prompt: A usable fully specified route was entered as shown. Which description is correct?
options: It requires ARP resolution for each host in the remote /16.
It names 10.0.13.2 as the remote destination prefix.
It forwards the /16 through Gi0/1 without using an IP next hop.
It directs the remote /16 to 10.0.13.2 through Gi0/1.
explanation: The destination and mask define 10.9.0.0/16; the interface and next hop jointly define its exit.

whyWrong.0: The Ethernet frame is addressed to the specified next hop, not individually to every remote IP.
whyWrong.1: 10.9.0.0/16 is the destination; 10.0.13.2 is the next router.
whyWrong.2: Both an exit interface and an IP next hop are explicitly supplied.

prompt: A completed traceroute from PC-A lists R1, R2 and PC-B. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The reverse data path must use exactly the same interfaces.
The trace reached PC-B and received its responses.
No route in the network can change.
Every application on PC-B is healthy.
explanation: A successful trace provides evidence about its probes and replies at that time. It is not a general application or symmetric-routing guarantee.

whyWrong.0: Replies can take another valid route.
whyWrong.2: Routes can change after the measurement.
whyWrong.3: Application services require their own tests.

prompt: How does an ordinary configured static route learn that a remote application has failed?
options: It does not provide an application health check by itself
It receives periodic updates from the static next hop
It polls that application whenever the metric is zero
It detects the failure from its configured prefix length
explanation: A static route defines forwarding information. Interface/resolution eligibility can affect installation, but an ordinary route is not an application monitor.

whyWrong.1: Static route statements do not establish a routing-update protocol.
whyWrong.2: Static metric zero does not configure an application probe.
whyWrong.3: A prefix describes destinations, not service health.

prompt: Only server 10.20.30.40 must use neighbor 172.16.1.2. Which route leaves other hosts in 10.20.30.0/24 unaffected?
explanation: The /32 host route matches only 10.20.30.40.

whyWrong.1: The /24 applies to the whole subnet.
whyWrong.2: The default covers all destinations without a more specific match.
whyWrong.3: The host bits are nonzero for that /24 network mask.

prompt: Gi0/0 is Ethernet. What consequence follows from this interface-only remote-LAN route?
options: R1 treats covered destinations as on-link and may ARP for each destination.
R1 automatically discovers the correct IP next hop using CDP.
The route is a connected interface route with code C.
R1 uses 192.168.20.0 as the next router address.
explanation: Without an explicit next hop, the Ethernet route can cause destination-by-destination ARP. This is unsuitable as the normal design for a remote LAN.

whyWrong.1: CDP does not fill in a missing static-route next hop.
whyWrong.2: The S code remains static; the display wording does not make it an interface-address-derived C route.
whyWrong.3: The prefix identifies destinations, not the next router.

prompt: An OSPF route to 10.5.0.0/16 has distance 110. Which TWO statements correctly describe a static backup to that same prefix?
options: Distance 5 makes the route less preferred than OSPF.
Distance 255 is the safest usable standby value.
The backup's next hop must still be usable when it is needed.
A usable backup can have distance 120.
explanation: The backup must lose the distance comparison while the preferred route exists, and must have a usable path when that route disappears.

whyWrong.0: 5 is lower than 110 and would be preferred for the same prefix.
whyWrong.1: Distance 255 is not installed as a usable route.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
Gi0/0: administratively down/down
No covering route to 10.0.12.2 in the installed table.

prompt: The only path to 10.0.12.2 was the now-down Gi0/0 connected subnet. No other route resolves it. Why is the configured next-hop-only route absent?
options: The remote network must use the transit link's /30 mask.
IOS cannot resolve the configured next hop.
A static route never installs until its destination answers a ping.
Static routes require a routing-protocol neighbor.
explanation: A recursive route requires a valid route that resolves its next hop. The stated resolving route is gone.

whyWrong.0: The destination mask describes the remote LAN independently of the transit subnet.
whyWrong.2: An ordinary static route does not test the destination with ping.
whyWrong.3: Static routing does not require a dynamic-protocol adjacency.

prompt: R1 and R2 have usable defaults pointing at one another and no other route covering 203.0.113.77. With ordinary forwarding and no filtering, what happens to a packet for that address?
options: The lowest next-hop address breaks the forwarding loop.
It can loop between the routers until its TTL expires.
The router with the lowest static AD becomes the final destination.
The default itself creates an Internet path.
explanation: Each lookup selects a default back to the other router. Each forwarding hop reduces TTL, limiting the loop.

whyWrong.0: Each router independently follows its default; next-hop address magnitude is not a loop-breaking rule.
whyWrong.2: Administrative distance selects sources locally; it does not make a router own the destination.
whyWrong.3: A forwarding instruction cannot create downstream connectivity.

prompt: Both displayed routes are installed. Which next hop handles 10.1.0.77?
options: 10.0.13.2, because /24 is the longer match
10.0.12.2, because distance 1 is lower
Neither, because a /32 is required
Both, because every overlapping route load-shares
explanation: 10.1.0.77 matches both prefixes. Forwarding selects /24, independently of the distances of different prefixes.

whyWrong.1: Distance is not compared between different installed prefix lengths for forwarding.
whyWrong.2: A network route covers all matching addresses.
whyWrong.3: Overlapping prefixes are not equal-cost paths to one identical prefix.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1: LAN 192.168.10.1/24, transit 10.0.12.1/30
R2: LAN 192.168.20.1/24, transit 10.0.12.2/30
R1 ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds; PC-A ping fails.

prompt: In the shown isolated lab, interfaces, host addressing and the outbound route are verified. R2 has no default or other route to 192.168.10.0/24. Which command on R2 fixes the missing return path?
options: ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1
explanation: R2 must route toward the PC-A subnet using R1's adjacent transit address, 10.0.12.1.

whyWrong.0: The host-mode gateway command does not create the required routed entry.
whyWrong.1: R2 already has the PC-B LAN connected; the missing destination is PC-A's LAN.
whyWrong.2: 10.0.12.2 is R2's own transit address, not its next hop.

prompt: Which R1 ping source specifically tests the return route to its LAN 192.168.10.0/24 when pinging remote PC-B?
options: 10.0.12.2, R2's transit address
192.168.20.12, PC-B's address
192.168.10.1, R1's LAN interface address
10.0.12.1, R1's transit address
explanation: A reply to 192.168.10.1 requires a route covering that LAN prefix. Select it through supported extended-ping options.

whyWrong.0: R1 cannot normally use another router's address as its own ping source.
whyWrong.1: The remote destination is not R1's source address.
whyWrong.3: A reply to the transit source tests a different prefix.

prompt: R1's primary interface remains up because it connects to a switch. A remote router beyond that switch fails. No tracking is configured. What should you conclude about the static backup?
options: Raising the backup distance enables remote-failure detection.
The primary may remain installed despite the remote failure.
Static routes exchange updates and will learn the failure.
The backup installs automatically whenever a remote ping fails.
explanation: Ordinary static routing does not provide an end-to-end health check. A local active interface can keep a fully specified route installed even when downstream delivery fails.

whyWrong.0: Distance changes preference rather than adding health monitoring.
whyWrong.2: Static routes do not exchange routing-protocol updates.
whyWrong.3: No probe tracking is configured, so failed pings do not themselves withdraw the primary.

prompt: The remote LAN is 198.51.100.64/26 and peer 10.0.12.2 is directly reachable. Which command names exactly that destination network?
explanation: The /26 mask is 255.255.255.192 and the aligned network starts at .64, covering .64–.127.

whyWrong.0: The /24 mask does not describe the requested /26 and .64 is not its aligned network.
whyWrong.1: That aligned /26 covers .0–.63, a different block.
whyWrong.3: A .65 destination has nonzero host bits for this /26 network route.

prompt: Which command removes the displayed backup while preserving the primary?
explanation: Match the backup’s prefix, mask, exit interface, next hop and explicit distance, then verify configuration.

whyWrong.0: This names a host route that is not the shown /24 backup.
whyWrong.1: This is the primary statement, which the task requires preserving.
whyWrong.3: This targets a different next-hop-only form and does not identify the shown backup.

prompt: R1 must reach the remote LAN through the adjacent R2 interface. Which next hop belongs in R1’s fully specified route?
options: 192.168.20.1, because it is the remote default gateway
192.168.10.11, because it is the requesting client
10.0.12.1, because it is R1’s sending interface
10.0.12.2, because it is R2 on the selected transit
explanation: For this directly adjacent fully specified path, the next hop is the peer on the selected transit link.

whyWrong.0: This is R2’s remote LAN interface, not the stipulated adjacent transit peer.
whyWrong.1: The client is the packet source, not the next routed hop toward the remote LAN.
whyWrong.2: R1’s own address is not the next router.

exhibit.title: Both configured candidates lose eligibility
exhibit.text:
R1 configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 5
Gi0/0 is down. The only route to 10.0.13.2 is also withdrawn.
No other route or default resolves either next hop.

prompt: The primary route is withdrawn. Which result follows from these complete eligibility observations?
options: The configured backup installs because its distance exceeds 1
The router creates a new next-hop route from the remote prefix
No route to the remote /24 can install from these candidates
Both statics remain installed because their configuration remains
explanation: The primary lost its required interface. The next-hop-only backup also has no valid resolving route. Preference cannot make an ineligible candidate usable.

whyWrong.0: A suitable distance is insufficient without a resolvable next hop.
whyWrong.1: The remote static cannot supply a valid independent path to its own unreachable next hop.
whyWrong.3: Configuration persistence does not establish installation.

exhibit.title: Failover with no reverse route
exhibit.text:
PC-A 192.168.10.11/24 → PC-B 192.168.20.12/24; both gateways correct.
After direct Gi0/0 link failure:
R1 installed S 192.168.20.0/24 [5/0] via 10.0.13.2 Gi0/1.
R2 Gi0/1 and both LANs are up; request delivery is observed.
R2 has no route or default for 192.168.10.0/24 after its Gi0/0 return route is withdrawn.
No filtering.

prompt: PC-A’s request reaches PC-B over the backup after the direct primary link fails. Which interpretation fits the complete evidence?
options: Different ADs in the two directions prevent replies from being forwarded
R1 must use a /32 instead of a /24 before PC-B can reply
R1’s outbound /24 is enough to establish R2’s route back to PC-A
R2 needs its own route to PC-A, and no such route remains installed
explanation: R1 has a working backup for the outbound destination, but R2’s only return route depended on the failed primary. The reverse destination needs its own eligible path.

whyWrong.0: Administrative distances are local preferences; opposite directions do not need matching values.
whyWrong.1: The /24 already delivered the request to PC-B. Its specificity does not create R2’s missing reverse route.
whyWrong.2: Forward and return route tables are independent.

exhibit.title: Equal-preference paths violate the standby policy
exhibit.text:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2
Both transits work. The installed /24 shows two static next hops at [1/0].

prompt: The policy requires Gi0/0 as primary and Gi0/1 as standby. What repair follows from the actual table and configuration?
options: Remove both routes and change the LAN mask to /25
Raise the Gi0/1 candidate’s distance above 1 for the same /24
Give Gi0/1 a more-specific /25 so it becomes less preferred
Increase the Gi0/0 route’s distance above the Gi0/1 route
explanation: Both statements omit an override and use AD 1, matching the observed equal-preference installed paths. Reconfigure the intended standby with a higher usable distance while preserving the prefix.

whyWrong.0: No addressing or primary-route failure is shown.
whyWrong.2: A more-specific installed prefix can attract traffic despite a higher AD.
whyWrong.3: That would prefer the intended standby instead of the primary.

exhibit.title: Construct matching primary and standby routes
exhibit.text:
Destination LAN: 198.51.100.64/26
Required primary: R1 Gi0/0 to directly adjacent 10.0.12.2
Required standby: R1 Gi0/1 to directly adjacent 10.0.13.2, AD 150
Both peers and the complete return path work. No other candidate for this /26 exists.

prompt: Which two configured candidates satisfy the stated network policy? (Choose two.)
explanation: The network and backup must describe the same /26. Default static AD 1 supplies primary preference; AD 150 is a usable lower preference and the named exits bind each candidate to its intended link.

whyWrong.1: This is a different /27 and can take traffic while the /26 primary is healthy.
whyWrong.2: AD 255 cannot supply an installed backup.
whyWrong.3: AD 200 would lose to the proposed AD 150 standby, reversing policy.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 routes:
C 192.168.10.0/24, Gi0/2
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
S 192.168.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
Complete relevant R2 routes (no default):
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
C 192.168.20.0/24, Gi0/2

prompt: All shown interfaces and PC gateways are correct, and no filtering is configured. PC-A at 192.168.10.11 pings PC-B at 192.168.20.12. Which result follows?
options: The request fails because R1 needs a /32 for every PC.
The request can reach PC-B, but R2 lacks a route for its reply to PC-A.
R2 learns the return route automatically from the received request.
Both directions work because the transit network is connected.
explanation: R1 has the outbound /24. R2 can deliver to its connected PC-B LAN but has no route covering the source LAN for the reply.

whyWrong.2: Receiving an ordinary packet does not install a reverse static route.
whyWrong.3: The reply destination is the PC-A LAN, not the transit subnet.

exhibit.title: Two transits share one destination-facing interface
exhibit.text:
R1 has /24 primary via R2 on Gi0/0 AD 1 and same-prefix backup via R2 on Gi0/1 AD 5.
Both transits stay up and the peer addresses remain reachable.
R2’s only interface into that destination LAN becomes administratively down.
No tracking or alternate route into that LAN exists.

prompt: Which two conclusions follow after R2’s LAN interface fails? (Choose two.)
options: R1 must withdraw the primary because the final LAN is unavailable
Changing the backup AD alone repairs R2’s failed LAN
R1’s default automatically replaces its still-installed /24
R1 can retain its installed primary even though delivery now fails
R1’s backup through the same R2 does not bypass the failed LAN
explanation: R1’s local primary transit remains eligible without remote tracking. Both paths terminate at the same R2, so neither avoids R2’s failed LAN interface.

whyWrong.0: The explicit local eligibility evidence remains true; no remote tracking is configured.
whyWrong.1: Preference changes cannot restore the destination interface.
whyWrong.2: A less-specific default does not replace a still-selected /24 for matching traffic.

exhibit.title: Alternate recursive next-hop resolution
exhibit.text:
R1 configuration:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2 5
Independent installed resolver after Gi0/0 failure:
S 10.0.12.2/32 [1/0] via 10.0.13.2, Gi0/1
The Gi0/1 peer is reachable and can reach 10.0.12.2.

prompt: After Gi0/0 fails, why can R1 still display the remote /24 at distance 1 rather than selecting its distance-5 candidate?
options: The primary is automatically converted into a fully specified route.
The next-hop-only primary can resolve through the surviving host route
Both static candidates must be installed whenever their prefixes match.
The backup /24 is more specific than the primary /24.
explanation: The primary is next-hop-only. The supplied independent /32 keeps its next hop recursively reachable through Gi0/1, so it can remain eligible at AD 1. A fully specified primary would bind it to the intended failed exit.

whyWrong.0: The configuration remains next-hop-only; alternate recursive resolution, not automatic conversion, explains the route.
whyWrong.2: For this same prefix the eligible AD-1 candidate remains preferred over AD 5.
whyWrong.3: Both candidates describe the identical /24; only the separate /32 resolves the primary’s next hop.

exhibit.title: Different ping results with incomplete evidence
exhibit.text:
R1’s ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds.
PC-A behind R1 cannot ping PC-B.
The engineer has not yet recorded R1’s ping source, PC-A’s gateway, or R2’s return routes.
No further fault evidence is supplied.

prompt: What is the most defensible next action before changing routing?
options: Compare the two test sources, host configuration and actual return routes
Raise all static distances to force a new path
Change PC-A’s mask so it includes the remote destination
Assume R2 lacks a return route and add a default immediately
explanation: The symptom suggests a source-dependent difference but does not uniquely identify its cause. Obtain the PC configuration and route back to its actual source before proposing a repair.

whyWrong.1: No source-preference defect has been established.
whyWrong.2: Broadening the LAN mask violates the addressing design and can create a new failure.
whyWrong.3: Missing reverse routing is possible, but the stated evidence does not yet establish it.
